Some thought experiments on AI art and the use of artworks and styles of digital artists:
So clearly it's not okay, lawfully or morally, to take a piece of art from RJ Palmer's Artstation, put it on your website, and sell prints of it for personal gain.

How different is this really from me theoretically being a talented digital artist, browsing Artstation for a few hours, finding RJ's work, then going into Photoshop and doing my best imitation? Is my creative mind not a similar black box of weights and activations?

An obvious difference here being effort, and the fact that in this thought experiment I am presumably some decently skilled digital artist who put time into both general artistic training, and the creation of this specific piece.
So take time and effort out of the equation. Suppose I am a talented programmer, and I spend years writing a perfect rules-based Python program that outputs very high quality RJ Palmer-esque work.

It is different from Stable Diffusion and other generative image models, since it was not trained directly on image data. It is rooted only in my interpretations of the logical rules that make RJ Palmer-esque artwork.
So the difference now is method of production (data vs. rules), and the loss of generality that comes without large training datasets.

But time/effort cannot be the limiter here, since if I open source this software, anyone can run and generate with little effort. Much effort went into building the system, but the artifacts it makes are cheap in terms of user/compute effort.

One thought is that in a perfect world we would have a sophisticated royalties lineage system that could trace the usage of copyrighted material in training data and pay accordingly when the resulting systems are used commercially
But again this feels at odds with the nature of learning to be creative. You are influenced by creative things in the world around you - your favorite artists, musicians, and writers.

Not sure what the conclusion here is, but in my mind the real scam is the free, centralized content distribution platforms where the datasets came from, not the generative models or datasets themselves.

Artists have to feed the beast to be seen, get work, and stay relevant.

PepperStake is a social accountability protocol which allows anyone to set and achieve goals by staking cryptocurrency.

Each PepperStake contract has 4 roles: creator, supervisor, participant, and sponsor.

The creator deploys the contract and sets its terms and parameters.

Participants stake crypto to complete the goal, a supervisor verifies whether the goal was completed for each participant.

Sponsors can pay the contract any amount to be split among completing participants. https://t.co/9oNo0K6zPN

This results in a powerful and flexible protocol which can be used for any of the following depending on its settings:

 🏃🏻‍♂️Individual goal setting
🎓 Group participation accountability
💪 1v1 competitions
⏰ Time-limiting reaching a consensus https://t.co/Ws9ccPDRG2

The PepperStake business model allows contracts to be deployed with a creator fee % and sponsor tip %.

Additionally, the protocol itself can be deployed with a fee % to be forwarded to the individual contracts.

💸

Future work includes building support for 

🦜 Oracle delegates - let another smart contract verify participants completed the goal
💰 Yield Generation delegates - Earn returns on crypto in escrow to share among completing participants

We intend to keep working on PepperStake in the coming months and we are seeking funding to build out the ecosystem.
